core: working definition of epidemic: an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area (CDC)
working definition of pandemic: an epidemic that has spread over several countries or continents, usually affecting a large number of people (CDC); the worldwide spread of a new disease (WHO)
the scale ladder: cluster and outbreak (local) to epidemic (regional) to pandemic (global); outbreak carries the same definition as epidemic but is used for a more limited geographic area
what makes a pandemic: geographic spread, not severity — neither official definition mentions how severe the disease is
the human story: epidemics are measured in people, not just numbers (1918 influenza as the example)
response differences: local and national health authorities for outbreaks/epidemics; international coordination through WHO for pandemics
honest framing: the words describe scale, not danger
supporting: sporadic (infrequent and irregular) and endemic (constant presence/usual prevalence) as the other end of the spectrum
baseline/endemic level as the expected level against which an epidemic is measured
non-infectious conditions (diabetes, obesity) can exist in epidemic proportion (CDC)
single case can warrant investigation for rare diseases (rabies, plague, polio — CDC)

1918 influenza pandemic figures: about 500 million infected (~one-third of world population), at least 50 million deaths worldwide, estimated 675,000 US deaths, greatest influenza death total in recorded history; four influenza pandemics in the last 100 years (1918, 1957, 1968, 2009); World War I conditions (overcrowding, troop movement) helped spread

WHO: viruses behind past pandemics were typically new, so most people lacked pre-existing immunity; pandemics tend to have higher overall impact partly because of the large number of susceptible people
outOfScope: outbreak investigation methods and traceback (owned by public-health:foundations:outbreak-investigation)
surveillance systems and case reporting mechanics (owned by public-health:foundations:disease-surveillance)
global health institutions and international health systems (owned by public-health:foundations:global-health)

claims.claim: The CDC defines an epidemic as an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.

The CDC defines an outbreak as carrying the same definition as an epidemic, but the term is often used for a more limited geographic area; a cluster is an aggregation of cases grouped in place and time suspected to be greater than the number expected.

The CDC defines a pandemic as an epidemic that has spread over several countries or continents, usually affecting a large number of people; the WHO describes a pandemic as the worldwide spread of a new disease.

Sporadic refers to a disease that occurs infrequently and irregularly; endemic refers to the constant presence and/or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area; the usual level is called the baseline or endemic level and is regarded as the expected level.
Pandemic status is defined by geographic spread, not by severity: neither the CDC nor the WHO definition of pandemic mentions how severe or deadly the disease is.
Epidemic language is not limited to infectious agents: non-infectious conditions such as diabetes and obesity exist in epidemic proportion in the United States, per the CDC.
For some rare diseases (e.g., rabies, plague, polio), a single case in a population warrants an epidemiologic investigation, per the CDC.

The 1918 influenza pandemic infected an estimated 500 million people worldwide — about one-third of the world's population — and killed an estimated 675,000 Americans and at least 50 million people worldwide, producing the greatest influenza death total in recorded history; there have been four influenza pandemics in the last 100 years (1918, 1957, 1968, and 2009), and World War I conditions such as overcrowding and global troop movement helped the 1918 virus spread.

The scale of a disease event shapes who coordinates the response: outbreaks and epidemics, being defined against a population and area, are handled mainly by local and national health authorities, while pandemics cross borders and draw in international coordination through organizations such as WHO, whose Global Alert and Response program tracks worldwide spread of new diseases.

conflictingEvidence.issue: In everyday usage, 'pandemic' is often taken to mean a disease that is extremely dangerous or deadly, but the formal definitions describe geographic spread.
positions: Popular usage treats pandemic as a synonym for catastrophic danger
CDC defines pandemic purely by spread over several countries or continents
WHO defines pandemic as the worldwide spread of a new disease
WHO notes pandemics tend to have higher overall impact partly because most people lack immunity, which can make severity follow reach in practice
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the formal CDC and WHO definitions: pandemic names reach, not deadliness. It states the spread-not-severity distinction plainly and adds the honest nuance that pandemics often do produce more total severe illness because so many people are susceptible.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Outbreak and epidemic are sometimes presented as categorically different events.
positions: Some informal sources treat outbreak as a small event and epidemic as a large one, as if they were different in kind
CDC states outbreak carries the same definition as epidemic, often used for a more limited geographic area
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the CDC ladder: the same rise-above-expected phenomenon at different geographic sizes, from cluster to outbreak to epidemic to pandemic.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained no factual claims; its boilerplate framing ('Epidemic Versus Pandemic is a foundational concept in Public Health') was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all machine-generated boilerplate with sourced working definitions (CDC/WHO) and original examples.
Definition of epidemic anchored to CDC's 'above what is normally expected in that population in that area' wording rather than a loose paraphrase.
Pandemic definition attributed to both CDC (epidemic over several countries or continents) and WHO (worldwide spread of a new disease).
1918 figures verified against CDC commemoration key messages (500 million infected, 50+ million deaths, 675,000 US deaths).

sourceRecords.title: What is a pandemic?
sourceRecords.provider: World Health Organization (WHO), Global Alert and Response
sourceRecords.notes: WHO page dated 24 February 2010; original who.int URL now returns 404 after the WHO site restructure, so the 2014 Wayback Machine capture was read. Supports: 'A pandemic is the worldwide spread of a new disease'; an influenza pandemic occurs when a new influenza virus emerges and spreads around the world and most people do not have immunity; viruses behind past pandemics typically originated from animal influenza viruses; impact/severity tends to be higher in pandemics in part because of the much larger number of people who lack pre-existing immunity. Used as reference only; facts synthesized in original wording.
